issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, 'institutional failure' and especially 'betrayal by someone trusted' are hard to reconcile unless the crash involved unusual interpersonal circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on fear/startle/intrusive sensory recall, which fits an accident trauma; these appraisal items instead imply an interpersonal or systemic-trauma narrative.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Guilt on recall' can occur after accidents, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the chosen appraisal set: the appraisals focus on betrayal/institutional failure rather than self-blame or responsibility. That makes the guilt theme insufficiently supported across nodes for a coherent cognitive formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the appraisal 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is hard to reconcile unless the crash specifically involved a trusted driver or intentional wrongdoing, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere else in the profile. As presented, it introduces a different interpersonal-trauma theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Self-Blame' can sometimes coexist, but in this profile they point to different causal narratives for the trauma (trusted other's betrayal vs one's own actions causing the event) without any supporting context. That makes the appraisal set clinically hard to unify around a single MVC trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: The profile contains a hard-to-reconcile blame pattern: strong self-blame and guilt are paired with other-blame rumination as a core maladaptive strategy. Mixed blame can occur, but this combination is the main internal inconsistency in the selected items because the appraisals and memory items point toward inward blame, while the strategy item points toward sustained outward blame.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, Maladaptive Strategies links most strongly to Negative Appraisals, so the strategy content should fit the appraisal style. Here the appraisal style is dominated by self-blame, helplessness, and permanent emotional damage, making other-blame rumination the least coherent strategy item.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, guilt on recall is plausible, especially with self-blame, so it is not problematic by itself. The concern is specifically its combination with persistent other-blame rumination, which pulls the profile toward a different blame direction than the rest of the formulation.

vignette: Juan had always been a man in motion. As a professional dancer, he spent most of his days moving to the rhythm of salsa and merengue music. But everything changed on that fateful night when his car skidded off the road, leaving him with severe injuries and a trauma that would haunt him for years to come. In the months following the accident, Juan found it increasingly difficult to sleep. He would stay up late, trying to distract himself from the memories that lingered in his mind like a specter. The sounds of screeching tires and shattering glass still echoed in his ears, making him feel like he was reliving the moment over and over again. When he did finally drift off to sleep, he would often wake up with a start, his heart racing as if he had been touched by an invisible hand. As Juan struggled to come to terms with what had happened, he began to experience intense feelings of shame whenever he recalled the accident. He couldn't shake the feeling that it was all his fault, that he was somehow responsible for the near-fatal collision. This sense of character blame only seemed to intensify as time went on, making him withdraw from his loved ones and avoid social situations. Juan's wife, Maria, noticed a change in him too. She would catch him scanning the room frantically whenever they entered a new space, as if searching for an escape route. And when she tried to touch him unexpectedly, he would flinch, startled by the sudden contact. Juan knew that these reactions were irrational, but he couldn't seem to shake them off. As the memories of the accident continued to haunt him, Juan found himself deliberately trying to dissociate from his body, as if leaving it behind could somehow free him from the trauma. He would blank out in the middle of conversations or while watching TV, only to snap back into reality with a jolt. This strategy offered temporary relief but ultimately made things worse, as he began to feel like he was losing touch with his emotions altogether. The more Juan tried to suppress his thoughts and memories, the more they seemed to resurface in unexpected ways. He would see flashes of the accident while practicing dance moves or hear the sound of screeching tires when someone honked their horn outside. These triggers only reinforced his negative appraisals – that he was helpless, that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. As Juan's maladaptive strategies intensified, so did his sense of threat and danger. He began to perceive the world as a hazardous place, full of potential risks and unknown terrors. This heightened state of alertness only served to further entrench his negative appraisals, creating a vicious cycle that seemed impossible to break. Juan knew he needed help when his avoidance behaviors started affecting his relationships with loved ones. He stopped attending dance performances, citing "injury" as the reason, but in reality, he was terrified of being in crowded spaces or performing under pressure. His wife and friends noticed the change in him too, and it was their concern that finally prompted Juan to seek professional help. As Juan sat in the therapist's office, recounting his story for the first time, he felt a sense of trepidation mixed with hope. He knew that confronting his trauma head-on would be painful, but he also sensed that this might be his only chance to break free from the cycle of fear and shame that had been holding him back for so long.
